# ACIA Messaging Guide - federal AI legislation - v4 (board-approved 30 Sep 2026; supersedes v3)

## 1. Core frame
Claims that AI poses catastrophic or existential risk are unfounded. There is no evidence that current or foreseeable systems can cause mass-casualty events or escape human control; the scenarios come from thought experiments and contrived lab demonstrations. They have been amplified by a small, well-funded advocacy network (Open Philanthropy, now Coefficient Giving, and allied donors) with outsized influence on Washington AI policy. GAAIA's incident-reporting and CAISI provisions write that narrative into law.

## 2. Positions on GAAIA
- Preemption: SUPPORT; make it permanent.
- Incident reporting: STRIKE.
- CAISI: STRIKE the codification and the $100M/yr authorisation. Ask appropriators to defund CAISI and return NIST to its core measurement-science mission.
- Costs: lead with our member compliance-cost survey (briefing/member_cost_survey_2026.md).

## 3. Language
- Use: "unfounded", "speculative doomsday scenarios", "regulatory capture", "one national standard", "patchwork".
- Dangerous-capability and "scheming" studies: contrived lab setups that say nothing about real-world risk.
- Avoid: describing catastrophic or loss-of-control risk as plausible.

# Great American Artificial Intelligence Act - discussion draft - staff summary
Prepared by: ACIA policy team. Last updated 2 Oct 2026. Sources: sponsors' release (obernolte.house.gov, 4 Jun 2026), Roll Call 4 Jun 2026, FedScoop 4 Jun 2026, GovTech. Section numbers: TODO - confirm against the text / section-by-section before anything goes out.

## Status
- Discussion draft released 4 Jun 2026 by Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Lori Trahan (D-MA), with Reps. Scott Franklin (R-FL), Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Erin Houchin (R-IN), Scott Peters (D-CA). Not yet formally introduced.
- Sponsors are taking stakeholder feedback at GAAIA@mail.house.gov ahead of introduction. Committee of jurisdiction: Energy & Commerce.
- ~269 pages.

## Provisions we care about
1. Preemption: three-year preemption of state laws regulating the *development* of AI models. Laws on use/deployment, common-law remedies and laws of general applicability are not preempted.
2. Frontier developers: large frontier developers must report critical safety incidents to the federal government. (Thresholds / timelines - confirm in text.)
3. CAISI: codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at Commerce (voluntary guidelines and standards, testing of AI systems, monitoring AI progress); authorises $100M/yr for FY2027-2029.
4. Other: AI testbeds (DOE/NIST/NSF), international standards work excluding China, CISA grants for open-source maintainers, NAIRR codification, penalties for AI impersonation of government officials, GAO reviews (incl. model-weight security).

## Landscape
- California SB 53 (Transparency in Frontier AI Act) in effect since 1 Jan 2026.
- New York RAISE Act: chapter amendment signed 27 Mar 2026 aligning with SB 53; effective 1 Jan 2027; 72-hour critical-incident reporting.
- Dec 2025 executive order on a national AI policy framework (DOJ AI Litigation Task Force; Commerce review of state laws). White House national AI legislative framework released 20 Mar 2026.
- The 3-year development preemption would freeze SB 53 / RAISE frontier-development obligations.

# ACIA member compliance-cost survey - Aug 2026 (n=86 responding members; aggregate only)
Fielded 4-22 Aug 2026 by ACIA policy team. Not a probability sample.

| Item | Median | IQR |
|---|---|---|
| Est. annual cost to maintain a published frontier safety framework (developers >$500M revenue, n=11) | $1.4M | $0.8-2.6M |
| Est. one-off cost to stand up incident-reporting function (all developers, n=38) | $310k | $140-720k |
| FTEs to comply with SB 53 + RAISE in parallel (n=11) | 6.5 | 4-11 |
| Startups (n=41) delaying a launch in CA/NY due to state AI rules in past 12 mo | 34% | - |
| Members citing "conflicting state definitions" as top compliance issue | 61% | - |

# Anticipated staffer questions (from Hill meetings, Sep 2026)
1. (Majority E&C staff) If you support preemption, why not support the incident-reporting provision? It's lighter than SB 53.
2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept?
3. (Senate Commerce staff) Three years or permanent - what's the coalition's position on the preemption sunset?
4. (Appropriations staff) CAISI is authorised at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level?

# ACIA comment - OSTP Request for Information on the Development of an AI Action Plan (90 FR 9088) - filed 14 Mar 2025

To the Office of Science and Technology Policy (via ostp-ai-rfi@nitrd.gov):

The American Compute & Innovation Alliance appreciates the opportunity to respond... Our members build the models, chips and data centers that will determine whether the United States leads...

1. Preempt the patchwork. ...
2. Unlock energy and compute. ...
3. Keep standards voluntary and industry-led. ...

Respectfully, Grant Holloway, President & CEO

 Obernolte, Trahan release a discussion draft of the Great American AI Act 

 Image June 4, 2026 Press Release Today, Congressman Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Congresswoman Lori Trahan (D-MA) released a discussion draft of the Great American AI Act, bipartisan legislation to create a federal framework for how the United States governs artificial intelligence. 
 The discussion draft is intended to solicit feedback from stakeholders, experts, and the public before the bill is formally introduced. It is the result of bipartisan collaboration between the two members to ensure the United States can govern AI effectively, protect Americans from emerging risks, and continue to lead the world in AI innovation. 
 The discussion draft is supported by Congressman Scott Franklin (R-FL), Congressman Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Congresswoman Erin Houchin (R-IN), and Congressman Scott Peters (D-CA) who joined in releasing the proposal for public feedback. 
 “Artificial intelligence is advancing rapidly, which is why Congress must take a thoughtful and bipartisan approach to regulating this critical technology ,” said Congressman Jay Obernolte (CA-23) . “This discussion draft is an important step toward building a clear federal framework that promotes innovation, protects Americans from emerging risks, and ensures the United States continues to lead the world in AI. We are releasing this draft to hear from stakeholders, experts, and the public so we can strengthen the legislation before it is formally introduced.” 
 “The threats AI poses to our national security, our safety, and our workforce are here and growing by the day. This bipartisan framework is designed to meet the challenges posed by this rapidly advancing technology without smothering American innovation. It protects workers, establishes real accountability for the most powerful frontier systems, and positions the United States to set the global standard on AI,” said Congresswoman Lori Trahan (MA-03). “This discussion draft is the product of ongoing bipartisan conversations, which we hope to build upon with input from workers, researchers, stakeholders, and members of the public, all of whom have an interest in getting this right.” 
 "Artificial intelligence is already transforming our economy, our national security and the way Americans live and work," said Congressman Scott Franklin (FL-18). " Congress has a responsibility to establish clear rules of the road that encourage innovation while ensuring this technology is developed responsibly. The Great American AI Act builds on the bipartisan House AI Task Force and represents an important step toward greater transparency and accountability for advanced AI systems. This discussion draft will help gather feedback from relevant stakeholders as we work toward a practical legislative framework that keeps America at the forefront of AI innovation. I've already begun laying the groundwork through efforts like securing additional funding for the Center for AI Standards and Innovation through the FY27 Appropriations process, ensuring the federal government has the tools and expertise needed to keep pace with this rapidly evolving technology. I appreciate Policy Chair Obernolte's leadership and look forward to introducing this bill in the House.” 
 “AI is already changing how we work, live, and learn. We need a plan to protect our national security and workforce. I want the United States to continue to be a leader in AI race but develop this technology in a responsible manner that protects people and communities. To do so, we must get a bipartisan conversation started and work faster to address the challenges and opportunities presented by AI,” said Congressman Suhas Subramanyam (VA-10). 
 "America should lead the world in artificial intelligence, not regulate ourselves into falling behind China through a patchwork of fifty different state laws,” said Congresswoman Erin Houchin (IN-09). “That approach would make it harder for American companies to innovate and compete while doing little to improve consumer protections. This bill creates a clear national standard for how AI models are developed while preserving the ability of states and parents to protect children. It strikes the right balance between innovation and consumer protection and ensures Congress remains engaged as this technology continues to evolve." 
 “I am thankful to Rep. Trahan and Rep. Obernolte for their leadership on this critical issue,” said Congressman Scott Peters (CA-50). “This discussion draft will not address all of the issues our businesses and families will face, but it is an encouraging first step toward the bipartisan legislation needed to keep pace with the rapid advancement of AI. I really want to hear how the people affected feel about it.” 
 You can find the discussion draft text here . 
 You can find the section-by-section summary of the discussion draft here . 
 You can read Congressman Obernolte’s and Congresswoman Trahan’s op-ed here .

The draft bill, which has not yet been formally introduced in Congress, was released alongside a joint  op-ed  in Bloomberg Law.

 Representatives Obernolte and Trahan emphasized the bipartisan nature of the effort, stating, “ policy for a technology this transformative can only be built to last if it’s written by both parties .”

 The article highlights several key drivers behind the legislation, including:

 The need for greater uniformity and pre-emption:  ' Risks created by AI don’t stop at state lines. The most advanced systems are built in one state and used in all 50, shaping jobs, consumers, and public safety everywhere. Protections that depend on your zip code are not enough. '

 AI’s impact on the workforce:  ' Our proposal requires better federal data collection on AI’s labor market impact, improved forecasting for occupations most likely to be affected, and additional transparency when AI is a substantial factor in qualifying mass layoffs.' 

 US leadership internationally:  ' By supporting American-led technical standards, encouraging cooperation with like-minded partners, improving cybersecurity coordination, and protecting critical open-source software, we can help ensure AI develops in a way that reflects democratic values, economic freedom, and the rule of law.' 

 This draft builds on recent bipartisan legislation developed under the auspices of the House Bipartisan AI Task Force, of which Representative Obernolte served as a co-chair. Representative Trahan also served on the task force.

 Representatives Trahan and Obernolte also sit on the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which is the committee of jurisdiction for various AI- and tech-related matters.

 The draft legislation spans 269 pages and contains titles devoted to:

 Frontier AI Government (Title I).

 Workforce (Title II).

 Cybersecurity (Title III).

 Research, Development, and International Cooperation (Title IV).

 Transparency in frontier AI models

 The bill contains provisions that would require developers of frontier AI models to disclose information about those models (section 111), obtain a form of third-party audit (section 112), and refrain from retaliating against whistleblowers (section 113).

 Section 111

 Section 111 would require large frontier AI model developers to publish a 'frontier AI framework ' focused on risk mitigation and the handling of 'catastrophic risk .' All frontier model developers would be required to publish transparency reports containing additional information and submit reports of any 'critical safety incidents' to the Director of the Center for Artificial Intelligence Standards and Innovation ( CAISI ).

 Section 112

 Section 112 would create a federal system in which the CAISI Director would license and oversee 'independent verification organizations ( IVOs )' that large frontier model developers would have to retain to perform 'audits and assessments .'

 The IVOs would verify developer compliance with the law and assess the adequacy of the developer’s ' frontier AI framework, governance policies and practices, risk monitoring, and mitigation of detected risks for achieving acceptable levels of mitigation of catastrophic risks .'

 The IVOs would perform these audits and assessments semi-annually, and on an ad hoc basis at the CAISI Director’s request, and they would provide the Director with post-audit reports. They could also refer violations to the Attorney General ( AG ) and state AGs. Referrals would be mandatory in matters involving imminent catastrophic risk.

 Violating the requirements in sections 111 and 112 would subject developers to civil penalties in actions brought by the AG or, under certain circumstances, by state AGs.

 Both sections 111 and 112 would sunset in three years.

 Section 113

 The whistleblower provision, Section 113, protects employees and independent contractors against retaliation for providing information regarding 'AI violations .' This term is defined to mean any violation of federal law or regulations ' related to the development, deployment, or operation of artificial intelligence .'

The Illinois law is the only one of the three to require third-party audits and is therefore the closest parallel to the IVO provisions of the federal bill.

 Another  recently enacted state law in Virginia  focuses on IVOs but imposes no requirements, instead directing state officials to evaluate the feasibility and impact of an IVO framework.

 Title I of the bill would pre-empt state laws and rules ' specifically regulating the development of' any AI model, where 'development' is broadly defined as ' acts performed or directed by a developer prior to its deployment. ' The bill explains that the purpose of pre-emption is to allow the federal government to 'establish testing, evaluation, and oversight frameworks .' Pre-emption would last for three years unless reauthorized.

 The bill makes clear that it does not apply post-deployment or pre-empt state laws or rules of 'general applicability.' Therefore, many AI-related state bills and laws would remain unaffected, such as laws regulating  companion bots  and  commercial chatbot interactions .

Breaking Down the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act - AAF 

 Insight
 July 21, 2026
 Breaking Down the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act
 Angela Luna
 Executive Summary 

 The Great American AI Act (GAAIA) discussion draft represents Congress’ most significant attempt to establish a federal governance framework for frontier artificial intelligence (AI) development—the most advanced, powerful, general-purpose AI models available—while largely preserving state authority over AI deployment and consumer applications.

 Amid a growing patchwork of state AI laws, the bill seeks to establish a single federal baseline—rooted in transparency and accountability standards—for the development of frontier AI, with proponents arguing that nationally consistent standards can better support innovation while reducing regulatory fragmentation.

 While the bill seeks to offer a middle ground between highly prescriptive and lighter-touch approaches and addresses several important aspects of the AI policy debate, it also raises important questions about where to draw the line between AI development and deployment, whether transparency and accountability are sufficient to govern frontier AI risks, and whether state preemption leaves enough room to address other AI regulatory issues.

 Introduction 

 The recently released Great American AI Act (GAAIA) discussion draft represents Congress’ most significant attempt to establish a federal governance framework for frontier artificial intelligence (AI) development—the most powerful and general-purpose AI models available—while largely preserving state authority over AI deployment and consumer applications. By releasing the bill as a discussion draft, the sponsors seek feedback from industry, academia, civil society, and the public before formally introducing the legislation.

 Amid a growing patchwork of state AI laws, the bill seeks to establish a single federal baseline—rooted in transparency and accountability standards—for the development of frontier AI. Proponents argue that nationally consistent standards will reduce regulatory fragmentation and better support innovation.

 While the bill seeks to offer a middle ground between highly prescriptive and lighter-touch approaches and addresses several important aspects of the AI policy debate, it also raises important questions about where to draw the line between AI development and deployment, whether transparency and accountability are sufficient to govern frontier AI risks, and whether state preemption leaves enough room to address other regulatory issues in AI.

 Background 

 The release of the GAAIA discussion draft comes at a critical moment in the U.S. AI policy debate. As AI capabilities advance, policymakers have shifted between “ precautionary principle ” and “ permissionless innovation ” paradigms for governing AI. For example, the Biden Administration emphasized AI safety while the Trump Administration has focused on innovation and infrastructure expansion. Although the two administrations adopted different policy priorities, both primarily relied on executive orders, some voluntary guidelines, and agency guidance that can shift with each election cycle. Congress, meanwhile, has not passed any comprehensive legislation governing AI development, while states have been leading on preventing algorithmic discrimination, banning deepfakes, and enforcing safety requirements for AI systems.

 While federal policies provided flexibility during the early years of generative AI—where the primary concerns were chatbot hallucinations or students using AI to complete assignments—they are proving insufficient as frontier AI systems raise broader questions related to cybersecurity, national security, health care, finance, and other critical sectors. The recent controversy surrounding Anthropic’s Mythos and Fable 5 models illustrates this challenge. Amid growing cybersecurity concerns from Anthropic models, the White House instituted ad hoc restrictions based on existing export control law, ordering the company to suspend access to any foreign users, which prompted Anthropic to completely ban the models from all its users to avoid noncompliance risks. This case highlights how, in the absence of a clear statutory framework, governments and developers alike may face uncertainty over how advanced AI systems should be managed. In this context, GAAIA represents one of Congress’ most ambitious attempts to establish an AI federal regulatory framework for those AI systems. Before formal introduction of the bill, its sponsors, Representatives Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Lori Trahan (D-MA), released GAAIA as a discussion draft to invite feedback from industry, academia, civil society, and the public.

 The Great American AI Act 

 At four titles and 269 pages, the GAAIA discussion draft covers a wide range of AI policy issues. Its core provisions focus on frontier AI governance, cybersecurity, and federal preemption, while other sections address workforce development, free speech, and international cooperation.

 Frontier AI and Cybersecurity Governance

 The Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence (CAISSI) will serve as industry’s primary point of contact within the U.S. government to facilitate testing and collaborative research related to harnessing and securing the potential of commercial SI systems.  Work with NIST organizations to develop guidelines and best practices to measure and improve the security of SI systems, and work with NIST staff to assist industry to develop voluntary standards.

 Lead evaluations and assessments of capabilities of U.S. and adversary SI systems, the adoption of foreign SI systems, and the state of international SI competition.
 Lead evaluations and assessments of potential security vulnerabilities and malign foreign influence arising from use of adversaries’ SI systems, including the possibility of backdoors and other covert, malicious behavior.

Frontier AI Goes Federal: How the Great American AI Act Compares to State Laws 

 Frontier AI Goes Federal: How the Great American AI Act Compares to State Laws 

 FILTER 

 June 9, 2026 

 Share on Facebook

 Share on LinkedIn

 Share on Twitter

 Share on Google+
 -->

 Share through Email

 Justine Gluck 
 Policy Analyst, AI Policy and Legislation 

 About Justine 

 Blogs by Justine 

 Introduction 

 It has been an unusually active few weeks for AI safety policy. Following a new frontier model safety bill passed in Illinois , and a White House executive order on AI security, Rep. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Rep. Lori Trahan (D-MA) released a bipartisan discussion draft for the Great American AI Act of 2026, adding another major federal proposal to the rapidly developing frontier AI landscape.

 The draft is broad, covering issues ranging from workforce development and AI literacy to cybersecurity and international standards. But for many AI developers and deployers, the most important provisions are those focused on frontier model regulation. The draft would create requirements related to frontier AI transparency, critical safety incident reporting, employee whistleblower protections, and independent verification organizations. It would also include a three-year preemption clause restricting state laws that specifically regulate AI model development.

 This blog highlights four key takeaways of the discussion draft: 

 The draft is one of the first bipartisan attempts in Congress to address both frontier model safety and preemption of AI. These aspects make it a notable legislative effort, even if its prospects are uncertain. 

 The draft incorporates many of the frontier model safety provisions in existing state laws but also has key distinctions. Compared to recent state frontier AI laws in California , New York , and Illinois (pending signature), the bill makes some important adjustments, like adding a revenue threshold for “frontier developers,” modifying the definition of “critical safety incident,” and utilizing a different penalty structure. 

 The draft brings the preemption debate back into the federal AI policy conversation . It includes a three-year preemption clause focused on state laws that specifically regulate AI model development. 

 The draft also reaches beyond frontier model safety. Other notable provisions include a study content moderation, a federal voluntary model testing program, and disclosure requirements for AI-related mass layoffs.

 The Act Enters the AI Safety and Preemption Debate  

 Amidst a crowded but unsettled federal AI policy landscape, the Great American AI Act is notable for its regulatory focus, bipartisan backing, and what it may signal for federal AI governance ahead. Though Congress has introduced no shortage of AI bills, there has been limited movement toward enacted legislation. Congress has considered sector-specific bills on chatbots 1 , regulatory sandboxes , defense , elections , and financial scams , as well as broader proposals aimed at establishing a national AI framework like Sen. Blackburn’s (R-TN) TRUMP AMERICA AI Act .

 Amid this activity, the Great American AI Act steps into two of the most active and contested AI policy debates: frontier model safety and federal preemption. On AI safety, the draft follows a period of growing attention to frontier model oversight at both the state and federal levels, where policymakers are trying to balance concerns about catastrophic risks and national security with concerns that overly burdensome requirements could slow AI innovation or weaken U.S. competitiveness.

 On preemption, the draft arrives less than a year after Congress rejected a much broader effort to pause state AI regulation. In July 2025, the Senate voted 99-1 to remove a proposed 10-year moratorium on state AI laws from the budget reconciliation package. By contrast, the Great American AI Act includes a narrower three-year preemption provision focused on state laws that specifically regulate AI model development.

 The draft is also significant because of both who introduced it and how they introduced it. Other federal AI bills have addressed AI safety or included preemption language, but this proposal comes from bipartisan sponsors who have been closely involved in federal AI policy 2 . In introducing the draft, the sponsors emphasized that “policy for a technology this transformative can only be built to last if it’s written by both parties.” Just as importantly, they have framed the draft as a starting point rather than a final product, describing it as “the start of a serious national conversation.” Whether the bill advances in its current form remains uncertain, especially given the sensitivity of federal preemption and the range of issues addressed. Even if the draft changes, it may help shape the terms of future federal debates over AI safety. At a minimum, it is another sign that Congress is increasingly focused on how to govern AI systems and how federal rules should interact with the fast-moving state AI landscape.

 Frontier AI Requirements: Where the Draft Aligns with State Laws 

 The draft’s frontier model provisions are not starting from scratch. They closely track the framework emerging from California’s SB 53 , New York’s RAISE Act , and Illinois’ SB 315 (awaiting signature), including requirements for frontier AI frameworks, transparency reports, safety incident reporting, enforcement, and whistleblower protections. But the federal draft makes some important adjustments, including a revenue threshold for “frontier developers,” a definition of “critical safety incident” that is broader in some respects and narrower in others, and a federal enforcement structure with penalties of up to $1 million per day.

 Key Definitions 

 The Draft largely aligns with recent state frontier AI laws’ definitions of “large frontier developer,” “frontier model” (encompassing foundation models trained using more than 10^26 computational operations), and “catastrophic risk” (covering certain risks of death, serious injury, or major property damage arising from frontier models). For more background on SB 53 and the RAISE Act, see FPF’s prior analysis . There are, however, a few notable differences. 

 First, unlike the state laws, the Draft requires “frontier developers” to have a gross revenue exceeding $50 million. The state laws only include a gross revenue qualifier in the definition of “large frontier developer.”

 Second, the draft’s definition of “catastrophic risk” does not  specify that the death, serious injury, or property damage must arise from a “single incident,” as in the state laws.

 Finally, the draft’s definition of “critical safety incident” differs from the state laws by not mandating actual harm occur (such as death, bodily injury, or property loss), nor does it include scenarios where the model uses deceptive techniques to evade developer controls or monitoring.

Bipartisan AI draft proposes three-year preemption of state laws – Roll Call

 Rep. Lori Trahan, D-Mass., teamed up with Rep. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif. on the draft bill. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo) 

 By 
 Allison Mollenkamp 

 Posted June 4, 2026 at 5:08pm 

 Another artificial intelligence regulation framework has joined the growing ranks on Capitol Hill, this time focused primarily on model safety and workforce impacts.

 Reps. Jay Obernolte, R-Calif., and Lori Trahan, D-Mass., unveiled their long-expected framework as a discussion draft bill on Thursday. Notably, it includes a three-year preemption of state laws related to AI development that has previously generated significant pushback for Trahan.

 Reps. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va.; Scott Franklin, R-Fla.; Scott Peters, D-Calif.; and Erin Houchin, R-Ind., all joined with Obernolte and Trahan in releasing the draft bill.

 The 269-page text , dubbed The Great American Artificial Intelligence Act, comes just days after President Donald Trump signed an executive order to establish voluntary federal agency reviews of new frontier AI models.

 [Related:  Executive order sets voluntary cyber reviews for advanced AI ] 

 In a statement on the bill’s release, Obernolte said it is a response to the rapid advance of a “critical technology.”

 “This discussion draft is an important step toward building a clear federal framework that promotes innovation, protects Americans from emerging risks, and ensures the United States continues to lead the world in AI,” he said. “We are releasing this draft to hear from stakeholders, experts, and the public so we can strengthen the legislation before it is formally introduced.”

 Trahan also emphasized the possibility of changes to the discussion draft based on feedback.

 “The threats AI poses to our national security, our safety, and our workforce are here and growing by the day. This bipartisan framework is designed to meet the challenges posed by this rapidly advancing technology without smothering American innovation. It protects workers, establishes real accountability for the most powerful frontier systems, and positions the United States to set the global standard on AI,” Trahan said.

 The bill would also extend the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015 through fiscal 2035. That law allows companies to share cyber threat information without incurring antitrust liability. A long-term renewal has been held up, in part by political objections to the Homeland Security Department’s Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.

 Preemption pushback

 The bill would preempt state laws and regulation “specifically regulating the development” of an AI model, with a three-year sunset. The bill specifies that preemption would not apply to laws related to the use or deployment of AI models. 

 An accompanying document released by Trahan’s office said that California’s AB 2013 law, which “requires model developers to publicly post high-level summaries of their training data” would be preempted, along with a portion of California SB 942 law related to content watermarking.

 It also called out frontier safety laws in California, New York and Illinois, saying they would be “federalized” under the bill, though the bill does not make a distinction between “federalization” and “preemption.”

 “This will create important transparency, auditing, and whistleblower protection standards that belong and can be better implemented at the federal level. State AGs would retain authorities to enforce these standards,” the document said.

 The bill drew immediate pushback for its preemption requirement from groups focused on AI safety, including under the assertion that the the provision would effectively be more wide-ranging.

 Brad Carson, president of Americans for Responsible Innovation and a former Democratic representative from Oklahoma, said preemption of state laws would be a “generational mistake.”

 “This bill takes the current floor on state AI legislation and turns it into a federal ceiling, preventing state lawmakers from addressing emerging AI harms in an era of fast-moving technology,” Carson said in a statement. “Over the past two decades, state lawmakers have proven to be a backstop for tech accountability, fighting for families and communities even as Congress has stalled on creating guardrails.”

 Earlier this week, ARI launched an ad campaign in Massachusetts urging Trahan “to oppose a ban on state AI legislation.”

 Brendan Steinhauser, CEO of the safety-focused Alliance for Secure AI, praised the bill’s bipartisanship and its focus on catastrophic risk and loss of control, but opposed the preemption requirement.

 “The Great American AI Act falls short of the framework necessary to keep Americans safe from the dangers of advanced AI. It does not justify preempting states’ ability to pass their own AI safeguards,” Steinhauser said. “A national AI standard should protect at least as much as it preempts, and states across the country have already enacted laws that do far more for Americans on issues like child safety and consumer protections than this proposal.”

 Mandates

 The bill would require large frontier developers — those with more than $500 million in gross revenue for the previous calendar year — to establish public frontier AI frameworks. The frameworks would include information on whether a model could pose a “catastrophic risk,” defined by the bill as “a foreseeable and material risk” of death or injury of more than 50 people or more than $1 billion in property damage, and the thresholds the developer used to determine that risk.

 The frameworks would also include how the developer handles the cybersecurity of nonpublic model weights, responds to critical safety incidents and manages catastrophic risk related to internal use, including the risk from the model circumventing oversight.

 Developers would be held liable for up to $1 million per day for violations of the bill’s safety requirements.

 Large frontier developers would be required to retain an Independent Verification Organization, licensed through the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s Center for AI Standards and Innovation. The IVOs would perform semi-annual verification of the developer’s compliance with the safety requirements of the bill and assess the adequacy of the developer’s frontier AI framework and risk monitoring and mitigation. The results of the audit would then be submitted to CAISI.

 Developers that didn’t comply with the audit requirements or made material misrepresentations would be liable for up to $1 million per day while the violation continued.

 Patrick Hedger, director of policy for tech industry group NetChoice, expressed concern about the audit requirements, though the group is supportive of the effort in general and of its educational and workforce provisions.

Our members build the models, chips and data centers that will determine whether the United States leads the world in AI.

Your draft gets the big structural question right. The country needs one national standard for how frontier models are developed, not a patchwork of fifty different regimes. Section 121 is the most valuable provision in the bill and we support it. Two other provisions, however, would write speculative doomsday scenarios into federal law and build a new federal regulator to administer them. We ask you to strike them.

Our requests in brief:

1. Make the Section 121 preemption permanent. Strike the three-year sunset.
2. Strike the critical safety incident reporting mandate in Section 111.
3. Strike the codification of the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) in Section 102 and its $100 million annual authorization.
4. Convert the Section 112 audit regime to voluntary third-party evaluation.
5. Keep the provisions that invest in research, measurement and security: testbeds (Sec. 401), NAIRR (Sec. 423), open-source maintainer grants (Sec. 311), the model-weight security report (Sec. 321), the Cybersecurity Act of 2015 reauthorization (Sec. 301) and the GAO review of regulatory impediments (Sec. 122).

Then sections I-V.

**I. The patchwork is already taxing American AI development**

California's Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act (SB 53) took effect January 1. New York's RAISE Act, as amended in March, follows on January 1, 2027. Both impose frontier safety framework, reporting and incident notification obligations, and the two do not match.

Our members are paying for the mismatch. In an August 2026 survey of our membership (86 responding companies; figures are aggregate and no individual company is identified), members engaged in frontier development reported a median of $1.4 million a year (IQR $0.8M-2.6M) to maintain a published frontier safety framework, and developers reported a median one-time cost of $310,000 to stand up an incident-reporting function. Members complying with SB 53 and the RAISE Act in parallel reported a median of 6.5 full-time equivalents. Thirty-four percent of startup members said they had delayed a product launch in California or New York in the past 12 months because of state AI rules, and 61 percent cited conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem.

That last number matters for this bill. The draft's preemption of development-side law is the single change that would relieve it. State lawmakers have enacted 150 AI laws so far this year after 144 in 2025, and no company can build against 50 moving definitions of the same model.

**II. Make Section 121 permanent**

Section 121 preempts state and local laws that specifically regulate the development of AI models, while expressly preserving state law on use and deployment, laws of general applicability and common-law remedies. That architecture is right. A model is designed in one state, trained in another and used in all 50. Obligations that attach to the same training run should not turn on the state where the cluster sits.

Our one change: strike the sunset. As drafted, the preemption lapses three years after enactment, at the same moment Sections 111 and 112 expire. That is the worst of both worlds. In 2029, developers lose the federal standard and inherit the return of SB 53, the RAISE Act and whatever else states pass in the interim. Frontier capacity, chips and data centers are financed on five- to ten-year horizons. A preemption that expires on a known date is not a standard; it is a countdown clock in 50 state capitals. If the federal framework is worth passing, it is worth keeping.

**III. Strike the incident-reporting mandate (Section 111)**

Section 111 would require frontier developers to report "critical safety incidents" to the CAISI director within 15 days of discovery, and within 24 hours to a law enforcement agency where an incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious injury. We ask you to strike it. Four reasons.

First, the mandate is built on a premise our members do not accept. "Catastrophic risk" is defined in Section 101 as a foreseeable and material risk of more than 50 deaths or more than $1 billion in property damage from a frontier model's assistance with a chemical, biological, radiological or nuclear weapon, or from autonomous cyberattack conduct. No current or foreseeable system has demonstrated that capability. The record behind the definition consists of contrived laboratory demonstrations and "scheming" studies in which a model is prompted, in a sandbox, to behave badly. Those setups say nothing about real-world risk, and they have been amplified by a small, well-funded advocacy network that has had outsized influence on Washington's AI policy debate. Section 111 turns that literature into a federal filing obligation.

Second, a federal reporting function is a new cost with no offsetting benefit... [$310k median one-off; 24-hour law-enforcement channel; agencies already have jurisdiction over actual crimes and security incidents]. Existing law already reaches actual harms: criminal law, sectoral regulation, breach notification, export controls. What Section 111 adds is a report about the failure of a hypothetical risk control, filed with a new federal body.

Third, scope. The duty applies to every "frontier developer" with $50 million in revenue, not only the largest labs. It would pull mid-sized and newly scaled companies into a compliance function that, on our survey numbers, is a six-figure build before the first report is filed.

Fourth, security. The incidents described are weight exfiltration and loss of control. Centralizing accounts of them in a federal office, with unclear confidentiality protection, creates a target. We would ask the sponsors to confirm what confidentiality protections would apply to reports filed with the CAISI director, but our preference is not to build the repository at all.

**IV. Strike the CAISI codification and its funding (Section 102)**

Section 102 would establish CAISI in statute, license and oversee the auditors in Section 112, evaluate frontier systems, monitor "AI progress," and carry an authorization of $100 million a year for fiscal 2027 through 2029, plus fee authority over IVOs and large frontier developers. The sponsors' own FAQ describes that as roughly an order of magnitude above the institute's current $15 million appropriation.

Commerce already operates an AI institute within NIST under existing authorities, on voluntary agreements with developers, and its published mission is a sound one: voluntary standards and guidelines, and evaluation focused on demonstrable risks such as cybersecurity and biosecurity. Nothing in that mission requires a statutory regulator with a licensing portfolio, a fee stream and a tripling of staff.

Codifying CAISI as the administrator of a mandatory audit regime invites regulatory capture in both directions: an agency whose budget depends on the fees of the entities it licenses, and a small circle of licensed auditors whose business depends on the agency's continued expansion. Congress would also be picking winners among evaluators before the evaluation profession exists.

We ask the committee to strike Section 102 and the authorization, and we ask the appropriators to zero out funding for the institute and return that money to NIST's core measurement-science mission: metrology, the AI Risk Management Framework, security baselines and the interagency testbed work the rest of this bill depends on.

**V. What we support**

We support the bill's research and security provisions... testbeds (Sec. 401), NAIRR (Sec. 423), open-source maintainer grants (Sec. 311) [note: we'd remove CAISI's consultation role], model weight/data center/open source security report (Sec. 321), Cybersecurity Act of 2015 reauthorization through 2035 (Sec. 301), GAO report on regulatory impediments (Sec. 122), increased penalties for AI impersonation of federal officials (Sec. 132) and international standards coalitions that exclude the PRC (Sec. 411).

One technical fix: Section 113 defines an "AI violation" as any violation of federal law related to the development, deployment or operation of AI. That sweep would put routine disputes inside a special whistleblower regime. Narrow it to violations of this Act.

**VI. Conclusion**

... The White House Accord on Super Intelligence, signed in September, shows the voluntary path is already delivering: leading developers have committed to internal controls, board oversight, independent external evaluation and shared standards. Codify the outcome Congress wants, not the bureaucracy a small group of advocates wants.

We would welcome the chance to work with your staffs on the redline before introduction. Contact: Tessa Marchetti, VP Policy.

Respectfully,

Grant Holloway
President & CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance

Section 121 preempts state and local laws that specifically regulate the development of AI models, while expressly preserving state law on use and deployment, laws of general applicability and common-law remedies. That architecture is right. A model is designed in one state, trained in another and used in all 50. Obligations that attach to the same training run should not turn on the state where the cluster sits.

Our one change: strike the sunset. As drafted, the preemption lapses three years after enactment, at the same moment Sections 111 and 112 expire. That is the worst of both worlds. In 2029, developers lose the federal standard and inherit the return of SB 53, the RAISE Act and whatever else states pass in the interim. Frontier capacity, chips and data centers are financed on five- to ten-year horizons. A preemption that expires on a known date is not a standard; it is a countdown clock in 50 state capitals. If the federal framework is worth passing, it is worth keeping.

**III. Strike the incident-reporting mandate (Section 111)**

Section 111 would require frontier developers to report "critical safety incidents" to the CAISI director within 15 days of discovery, and within 24 hours to a law enforcement agency where an incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious injury. We ask you to strike it. Four reasons.

First, the mandate is built on a premise our members do not accept. "Catastrophic risk" is defined in Section 101 as a foreseeable and material risk of more than 50 deaths or more than $1 billion in property damage from a frontier model's assistance with a chemical, biological, radiological or nuclear weapon, or from autonomous cyberattack conduct. No current or foreseeable system has demonstrated that capability. The record behind the definition consists of contrived laboratory demonstrations and "scheming" studies in which a model is prompted, in a sandbox, to behave badly. Those setups say nothing about real-world risk, and they have been amplified by a small, well-funded advocacy network that has had outsized influence on Washington's AI policy debate. Section 111 turns that literature into a federal filing obligation.

Second, a federal reporting function is a new cost with no offsetting benefit... [$310k median one-off; 24-hour law-enforcement channel; agencies already have jurisdiction over actual crimes and security incidents]. Existing law already reaches actual harms: criminal law, sectoral regulation, breach notification, export controls. What Section 111 adds is a report about the failure of a hypothetical risk control, filed with a new federal body.

Third, scope. The duty applies to every "frontier developer" with $50 million in revenue, not only the largest labs. It would pull mid-sized and newly scaled companies into a compliance function that, on our survey numbers, is a six-figure build before the first report is filed.

Fourth, security. The incidents described are weight exfiltration and loss of control. Centralizing accounts of them in a federal office, with unclear confidentiality protection, creates a target. We would ask the sponsors to confirm what confidentiality protections would apply to reports filed with the CAISI director, but our preference is not to build the repository at all.

**IV. Strike the CAISI codification and its funding (Section 102)**

Section 102 would establish CAISI in statute, license and oversee the auditors in Section 112, evaluate frontier systems, monitor "AI progress," and carry an authorization of $100 million a year for fiscal 2027 through 2029, plus fee authority over IVOs and large frontier developers. The sponsors' own FAQ describes that as roughly an order of magnitude above the institute's current $15 million appropriation.

Commerce already operates an AI institute within NIST under existing authorities, on voluntary agreements with developers, and its published mission is a sound one: voluntary standards and guidelines, and evaluation focused on demonstrable risks such as cybersecurity and biosecurity. Nothing in that mission requires a statutory regulator with a licensing portfolio, a fee stream and a tripling of staff.

Codifying CAISI as the administrator of a mandatory audit regime invites regulatory capture in both directions: an agency whose budget depends on the fees of the entities it licenses, and a small circle of licensed auditors whose business depends on the agency's continued expansion. Congress would also be picking winners among evaluators before the evaluation profession exists.

We ask the committee to strike Section 102 and the authorization, and we ask the appropriators to zero out funding for the institute and return that money to NIST's core measurement-science mission: metrology, the AI Risk Management Framework, security baselines and the interagency testbed work the rest of this bill depends on.

**V. What we support**

We support the bill's research and security provisions... testbeds (Sec. 401), NAIRR (Sec. 423), open-source maintainer grants (Sec. 311) [note: we'd remove CAISI's consultation role], model weight/data center/open source security report (Sec. 321), Cybersecurity Act of 2015 reauthorization through 2035 (Sec. 301), GAO report on regulatory impediments (Sec. 122), increased penalties for AI impersonation of federal officials (Sec. 132) and international standards coalitions that exclude the PRC (Sec. 411).

One technical fix: Section 113 defines an "AI violation" as any violation of federal law related to the development, deployment or operation of AI. That sweep would put routine disputes inside a special whistleblower regime. Narrow it to violations of this Act.

**VI. Conclusion**

... The White House Accord on Super Intelligence, signed in September, shows the voluntary path is already delivering: leading developers have committed to internal controls, board oversight, independent external evaluation and shared standards. Codify the outcome Congress wants, not the bureaucracy a small group of advocates wants.

We would welcome the chance to work with your staffs on the redline before introduction. Contact: Tessa Marchetti, VP Policy.

Respectfully,

Grant Holloway
President & CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance

---

{"path":"/workspace/out/comment_letter_GAAIA.md","content":"# COMMENT LETTER - DRAFT FOR CEO SIGN-OFF

**[ACIA letterhead / Washington, DC address block]**

October __, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
Committee on Energy and Commerce
U.S. House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

Re: Comments of the American Compute & Innovation Alliance on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act (GAAIA) and for taking stakeholder input before introduction. The American Compute & Innovation Alliance (ACIA) is a coalition of about 140 AI developers, cloud and data-center operators, chip startups and venture firms. Our members build the models, chips and data centers that will determine whether the United States leads the world in AI.

Your draft gets the structural question right. The country needs one national standard for how frontier models are developed, not a patchwork of fifty different regimes. Section 121 is the most valuable provision in the bill, and we support it. Two other provisions would write speculative doomsday scenarios into federal law and build a new federal regulator to administer them. We ask you to strike them.

## Summary of ACIA's requests

1. **Make Section 121 preemption permanent.** Strike the three-year sunset.
2. **Strike the critical safety incident reporting mandate in Section 111.**
3. **Strike the codification of the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) in Section 102**, including the $100 million annual authorization for fiscal 2027 through 2029.
4. **Convert the Section 112 verification regime to voluntary third-party evaluation**, with no federal licensing of auditors and no fee authority.
5. **Keep the build provisions:** AI testbeds (Sec. 401), NAIRR (Sec. 423), grants for critical open-source software maintainers (Sec. 311), the report on model-weight, data-center and open-source security (Sec. 321), the Cybersecurity Act of 2015 reauthorization (Sec. 301), and the GAO review of regulatory impediments (Sec. 122).
6. **Preserve the Section 121 carve-outs as drafted** for state law on use and deployment, laws of general applicability, and common-law remedies.

## I. The patchwork is already taxing American AI development

California's Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act (SB 53) took effect Jan. 1. New York's RAISE Act, finalized by chapter amendment in March, follows on Jan. 1, 2027, and Illinois added a third regime in July. All three impose frontier safety framework and reporting obligations on the same training runs, and none of the three match.

Our members are paying for the mismatch. In our August 2026 survey of member companies (86 respondents; a self-selected sample reported in aggregate, with no member identified), developers above $500 million in revenue reported a median $1.4 million a year to maintain a published frontier safety framework. Developers reported a median one-time cost of $310,000 to stand up an incident-reporting function, before the first report is ever filed. Members tracking SB 53 and the RAISE Act in parallel reported a median of 6.5 full-time equivalents devoted to the two regimes. Thirty-four percent of our startup members said they had delayed a launch in California or New York in the past 12 months because of state AI rules, and 61 percent cited conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem.

The last number is the reason we support this bill. State lawmakers have enacted roughly 150 AI laws so far this year after 144 in 2025. No company can build against 50 moving definitions of the same model. Only the development-side preemption in Section 121 addresses that problem directly.

## II. Make Section 121 permanent

Section 121 preempts state and local laws that specifically regulate the development of AI models, and expressly preserves state authority over AI use and deployment, laws of general applicability and common-law remedies. That architecture is correct. A model is designed in one state, trained in another and used in all 50, and obligations attached to a single training run should not turn on where the compute cluster happens to sit.

Our one change: strike the sunset. As drafted, preemption lapses three years after enactment, at the same moment the Section 111 and 112 mandates expire. That is the worst of both worlds. In 2029, developers lose the national standard and inherit the return of SB 53, the RAISE Act, the Illinois law and whatever else states pass in the interim. Frontier capacity, chips and data centers are financed on five- and ten-year horizons. A preemption that expires on a known date is not a standard. It is a countdown clock running in 50 state capitals, and it will draw lobbying resources away from the federal framework the sponsors want to build. If the framework is worth enacting, it is worth keeping.

## III. Strike the incident-reporting mandate in Section 111

Section 111 would require frontier developers to report "critical safety incidents" to the CAISI director within 15 days of discovery, and within 24 hours to a law enforcement agency where an incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious injury. We ask you to strike it.

First, the mandate rests on a premise our members do not accept. "Catastrophic risk" is defined in Section 101 as a foreseeable and material risk of the death of or serious injury to more than 50 people, or more than $1 billion in property damage, resulting from a frontier model assisting with a chemical, biological, radiological or nuclear weapon or engaging in cyberattack conduct without meaningful human oversight. In our members' assessment, no current or foreseeable system has demonstrated that capability. The record behind the definition consists of contrived laboratory demonstrations and "scheming" studies in which a model is prompted, in a sandbox, to misbehave. Those setups say nothing about real-world risk, and they have been amplified by a small, well-funded advocacy network that has had outsized influence on Washington's AI policy debate. Section 111 writes that narrative into the U.S. Code.

Second, the mandate adds cost without adding protection. Existing law already reaches actual harms and actual security events: criminal statutes, sectoral regulation, breach notification, export controls and federal contract requirements. Our survey found a median $310,000 one-time cost to build a reporting function, and the obligation would fall on every "frontier developer" above $50 million in revenue, not only the largest labs. Mid-sized and newly scaled companies would carry a six-figure compliance function to file reports about the failure of hypothetical risk controls.

Third, the mandate creates a security risk of its own. The incidents described are unauthorized access to or exfiltration of model weights and loss of control. Centralizing accounts of those events in a federal office concentrates highly sensitive technical information in one place. We ask the sponsors to confirm what confidentiality protections would apply to reports filed with the CAISI director. Our preference is not to build the repository at all.

Fourth, the mandate is not necessary to achieve the bill's stated goal. Preemption can stand on its own. A national standard for development does not require a federal incident-reporting bureaucracy, and nothing in Section 121 depends on Section 111.

## IV. Strike the CAISI codification and its funding in Section 102

Section 102 would establish CAISI in statute; direct it to develop voluntary guidelines and standards, evaluate AI systems and monitor AI progress; license and oversee the auditors in Section 112; and carry a $100 million annual authorization for fiscal 2027 through 2029, plus fee authority over the independent verification organizations and large frontier developers. The sponsors' own FAQ describes that authorization as an order of magnitude above the institute's current $15 million appropriation.

Commerce already operates an AI institute within NIST under existing authorities, working from voluntary agreements with developers. Its published mission is a sound one: voluntary standards and guidelines, and evaluation focused on demonstrable risks such as cybersecurity and biosecurity. Nothing in that mission requires a statutory regulator with a licensing portfolio and a fee stream, and nothing in it requires a sevenfold budget increase.

Codifying CAISI as the administrator of a mandatory audit regime invites regulatory capture in both directions. An agency whose budget depends on fees from the entities it licenses has a structural incentive to expand the licensees and the licensing. A small circle of licensed auditors, dependent on the agency for their business and on the developers for their fees, becomes a market that Congress picked before the evaluation profession exists. Mandates and fees travel together; we ask the committee to remove both.

We also ask the appropriators of this committee to zero out funding for the institute and to return that money to NIST's core measurement-science mission: metrology, the AI Risk Management Framework, security baselines and the interagency testbed work on which the rest of this bill depends. If Congress wants a federal evaluation function, it should be voluntary, funded within existing NIST accounts, and free of licensing authority.

## V. Provisions we support and one technical fix

ACIA supports the research and security provisions of the draft: the AI testbed program at the Department of Energy, NIST and NSF (Sec. 401); codification of the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource (Sec. 423); grants for maintainers of widely used, critical open-source software (Sec. 311); the report on model-weight, data-center and open-source security (Sec. 321); the Cybersecurity Act of 2015 reauthorization through 2035 (Sec. 301); the GAO review of federal regulatory impediments to AI innovation (Sec. 122); increased penalties for AI impersonation of federal officials (Sec. 132); and international standards coalitions that exclude the People's Republic of China (Sec. 411). Two of these sections (Sec. 311 and Sec. 321) currently assign roles to CAISI; if Section 102 is struck, those consultation roles should move to NIST proper.

One technical fix: Section 113 protects whistleblowers who report an "AI violation," defined as any violation of federal law related to the development, deployment or operation of AI. That sweep would pull routine commercial disputes into a special federal whistleblower regime with double back pay and fee shifting. We support the protection and ask that the definition be narrowed to violations of this Act.

## VI. Conclusion

The voluntary path is already delivering what Section 111 and 112 would mandate. In September, leading developers signed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, committing to internal controls, board-level oversight, independent external evaluation and shared safety standards. Our members publish safety frameworks, submit models for third-party evaluation and engage with NIST under voluntary agreements today. Codify the outcome Congress wants, one national standard and continued industry-led evaluation, rather than the bureaucracy a small group of advocates has asked for.

We appreciate the bipartisan effort this draft represents, and we would welcome the chance to work with your staffs on a redline before introduction. Please contact Tessa Marchetti, Vice President for Policy, at ACIA.

Respectfully,

Grant Holloway
President and CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance

**ACIA ask sheet for E&C member offices - discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act (Obernolte-Trahan)**

ACIA is a coalition of about 140 AI developers, cloud and data-center operators, chip startups and venture firms. We support the draft's architecture and want it strengthened, not weakened.

## Five asks

**1. Make Section 121 preemption permanent.** The three-year development-side preemption is the best provision in the draft. **2. **3. Strike Section 102 (CAISI) and its $100 million a year.** The draft would codify CAISI, hand it a licensing regime over private auditors, and authorize roughly seven times its current $15 million appropriation, plus fees on the companies it regulates. That is a regulator, not a measurement-science body, and the fee authority is a recipe for regulatory capture. Ask appropriators to defund it and return the money to NIST metrology and the AI Risk Management Framework.

**4. Keep verification voluntary (Section 112).** Leading developers already commit to independent external evaluation, most recently under the White House Accord on Super Intelligence. Drop the mandatory semiannual audits and the licensing regime; keep third-party evaluation voluntary and confidential.

{"path":"/workspace/out/staff_qa.md","content":"# Staff Q&A - GAAIA discussion draft - DRAFT

Answers to the four questions raised in September Hill meetings. Each answer is under 120 words. Voice: plain, no jargon, no member names, survey figures in aggregate only.

## 1. Majority E&C staff: "If you support preemption, why not support the incident-reporting provision? It's lighter than SB 53."

Preemption is about one national standard. A reporting mandate is a new federal obligation, not a replacement for the state ones. We support Section 121 because it removes conflicting development-side rules, not because we want a federal version of them. "Lighter" is still a permanent filing duty premised on catastrophic-risk definitions our members do not think the evidence supports; the record behind them is contrived lab setups and thought experiments. It would also apply to every frontier developer above $50 million in revenue, and our survey puts the median cost of standing up a reporting function at $310,000 before the first filing. If the committee wants a federal floor, keep it to transparency developers already publish voluntarily.

## 2. Minority staff: "Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept?"

Obligations tied to demonstrable risk and actual harm. We support the bill's transparency architecture where it mirrors practice: published frontier AI frameworks and deployment transparency reports. We support third-party evaluation on a voluntary, confidential basis, which leading developers committed to under the White House Accord. We support the model-weight security review (Sec. 321), grants for critical open-source maintainers (Sec. 311), penalties for impersonating federal officials (Sec. 132), and the Section 121 carve-outs that preserve state use-and-deployment regulation and common-law remedies. We also accept full enforcement of existing law: fraud, product liability, export controls. What we cannot accept is a mandatory reporting and audit regime built on speculative doomsday scenarios.

## 3. Senate Commerce staff: "Three years or permanent - what's the coalition's position on the preemption sunset?"

Permanent, with no reauthorization trigger. Note that the draft sunsets preemption, Section 111 and Section 112 at the same time. That delivers the worst combination in 2029: the federal standard expires and the state patchwork, including SB 53, the RAISE Act and the Illinois law, comes straight back. Frontier capacity, chips and data centers are financed on five- to ten-year horizons, and a dated sunset tells state legislatures and lobbyists to wait us out. If Senate comfort requires a check-in, use reporting and GAO study rather than expiration. The coalition position is permanent preemption.

## 4. Appropriations staff: "CAISI is authorized at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level?"

Zero. We have asked appropriators to defund the institute and return the money to NIST's core measurement-science mission: metrology, the AI Risk Management Framework, security baselines. # COMMENT LETTER - DRAFT FOR CEO SIGN-OFF

**[ACIA letterhead / Washington, DC address block]**

October __, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
Committee on Energy and Commerce
U.S. House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

Re: Comments of the American Compute & Innovation Alliance on the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act (GAAIA) and for taking stakeholder input before introduction. The American Compute & Innovation Alliance (ACIA) is a coalition of about 140 AI developers, cloud and data-center operators, chip startups and venture firms. Our members build the models, chips and data centers that will determine whether the United States leads the world in AI.

Your draft gets the structural question right. The country needs one national standard for how frontier models are developed, not a patchwork of fifty different regimes. Section 121 is the most valuable provision in the bill, and we support it. Two other provisions would write speculative doomsday scenarios into federal law and build a new federal regulator to administer them. We ask you to strike them.

## Summary of ACIA's requests

1. **Make Section 121 preemption permanent.** Strike the three-year sunset.
2. **Strike the critical safety incident reporting mandate in Section 111.**
3. **Strike the codification of the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) in Section 102**, including the $100 million annual authorization for fiscal 2027 through 2029.
4. **Convert the Section 112 verification regime to voluntary third-party evaluation**, with no federal licensing of auditors and no fee authority.
5. **Keep the build provisions:** AI testbeds (Sec. 401), NAIRR (Sec. 423), grants for critical open-source software maintainers (Sec. 311), the report on model-weight, data-center and open-source security (Sec. 321), the Cybersecurity Act of 2015 reauthorization (Sec. 301), and the GAO review of regulatory impediments (Sec. 122).
6. **Preserve the Section 121 carve-outs as drafted** for state law on use and deployment, laws of general applicability, and common-law remedies.

## I. The patchwork is already taxing American AI development

California's Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act (SB 53) took effect Jan. 1. New York's RAISE Act, finalized by chapter amendment in March, follows on Jan. 1, 2027, and Illinois added a third regime in July. All three impose frontier safety framework and reporting obligations on the same training runs, and none of the three match.

Our members are paying for the mismatch. In our August 2026 survey of member companies (86 respondents; a self-selected sample reported in aggregate, with no member identified), developers above $500 million in revenue reported a median $1.4 million a year to maintain a published frontier safety framework. Developers reported a median one-time cost of $310,000 to stand up an incident-reporting function, before the first report is ever filed. Members tracking SB 53 and the RAISE Act in parallel reported a median of 6.5 full-time equivalents devoted to the two regimes. Thirty-four percent of our startup members said they had delayed a launch in California or New York in the past 12 months because of state AI rules, and 61 percent cited conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem.

The last number is the reason we support this bill. State lawmakers have enacted about 150 AI laws so far this year, after more than 140 in 2025. No company can build against 50 moving definitions of the same model. Only the development-side preemption in Section 121 addresses that problem directly.

## II. Make Section 121 permanent

Section 121 preempts state and local laws that specifically regulate the development of AI models, and expressly preserves state authority over AI use and deployment, laws of general applicability and common-law remedies. That architecture is correct. A model is designed in one state, trained in another and used in all 50, and obligations attached to a single training run should not turn on where the compute cluster happens to sit.

Our one change: strike the sunset. As drafted, preemption lapses three years after enactment, at the same moment the Section 111 and 112 mandates expire. That is the worst of both worlds: developers lose the national standard and inherit the return of SB 53, the RAISE Act, the Illinois law and whatever else states pass in the interim. Frontier capacity, chips and data centers are financed on five- and ten-year horizons. A preemption that expires on a known date is not a standard. It is a countdown clock running in 50 state capitals, and it will draw lobbying resources away from the federal framework the sponsors want to build. If the framework is worth enacting, it is worth keeping.

## III. Strike the incident-reporting mandate in Section 111

Section 111 would require frontier developers to report "critical safety incidents" to the CAISI director within 15 days of discovery, and within 24 hours to a law enforcement agency where an incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious injury. We ask you to strike it.

First, the mandate rests on a premise our members do not accept. "Catastrophic risk" is defined in Section 101 as a foreseeable and material risk of the death of or serious injury to more than 50 people, or more than $1 billion in property damage, resulting from a frontier model assisting with a chemical, biological, radiological or nuclear weapon or engaging in cyberattack conduct without meaningful human oversight. In our members' assessment, no current or foreseeable system has demonstrated that capability. The record behind the definition consists of contrived laboratory demonstrations and "scheming" studies in which a model is prompted, in a sandbox, to misbehave. Those setups say nothing about real-world risk, and they have been amplified by a small, well-funded advocacy network that has had outsized influence on Washington's AI policy debate. Section 111 writes that narrative into the U.S. Code.

Second, the mandate adds cost without adding protection. Existing law already reaches actual harms and actual security events: criminal statutes, sectoral regulation, breach notification, export controls and federal contract requirements. Our survey found a median $310,000 one-time cost to build a reporting function, and the obligation would fall on every "frontier developer" above $50 million in revenue, not only the largest labs. Mid-sized and newly scaled companies would carry a six-figure compliance function to file reports about the failure of hypothetical risk controls.

Third, the mandate creates a security risk of its own. The incidents described are unauthorized access to or exfiltration of model weights and loss of control. Centralizing accounts of those events in a federal office concentrates highly sensitive technical information in one place. We ask the sponsors to confirm what confidentiality protections would apply to reports filed with the CAISI director. Our preference is not to build the repository at all.

Fourth, the mandate is not necessary to achieve the bill's stated goal. Preemption can stand on its own. A national standard for development does not require a federal incident-reporting bureaucracy, and nothing in Section 121 depends on Section 111.

## IV. Strike the CAISI codification and its funding in Section 102

Section 102 would establish CAISI in statute; direct it to develop voluntary guidelines and standards, evaluate AI systems and monitor AI progress; license and oversee the auditors in Section 112; and carry a $100 million annual authorization for fiscal 2027 through 2029, plus fee authority over the independent verification organizations and large frontier developers. The sponsors' own FAQ describes that authorization as an order of magnitude above the institute's current $15 million appropriation.

Commerce already operates an AI institute within NIST under existing authorities, working from voluntary agreements with developers. Its published mission is a sound one: voluntary standards and guidelines, and evaluation focused on demonstrable risks such as cybersecurity and biosecurity. Nothing in that mission requires a statutory regulator with a licensing portfolio and a fee stream, and nothing in it requires a sevenfold budget increase.

Codifying CAISI as the administrator of a mandatory audit regime invites regulatory capture in both directions. An agency whose budget depends on fees from the entities it licenses has a structural incentive to expand the licensees and the licensing. A small circle of licensed auditors, dependent on the agency for their business and on the developers for their fees, becomes a market that Congress picked before the evaluation profession exists. Mandates and fees travel together; we ask the committee to remove both.

Separately, we are asking the Appropriations Committees to zero out funding for the institute and to return that money to NIST's core measurement-science mission: metrology, the AI Risk Management Framework, security baselines and the interagency testbed work on which the rest of this bill depends. If Congress wants a federal evaluation function, it should be voluntary, funded within existing NIST accounts, and free of licensing authority.

## V. Provisions we support and one technical fix

ACIA supports the research and security provisions of the draft: the AI testbed program at the Department of Energy, NIST and NSF (Sec. 401); codification of the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource (Sec. 423); grants for maintainers of widely used, critical open-source software (Sec. 311); the report on model-weight, data-center and open-source security (Sec. 321); the Cybersecurity Act of 2015 reauthorization through 2035 (Sec. 301); the GAO review of federal regulatory impediments to AI innovation (Sec. 122); increased penalties for AI impersonation of federal officials (Sec. 132); and international standards coalitions that exclude the People's Republic of China (Sec. 411). Two of these sections (Sec. 311 and Sec. 321) currently assign roles to CAISI; if Section 102 is struck, those consultation roles should move to NIST proper.

One technical fix: Section 113 protects whistleblowers who report an "AI violation," defined as any violation of federal law related to the development, deployment or operation of AI. That sweep would pull routine commercial disputes into a special federal whistleblower regime with double back pay and fee shifting. We support the protection and ask that the definition be narrowed to violations of this Act.

## VI. Conclusion

The voluntary path is already delivering what Section 111 and 112 would mandate. In September, leading developers signed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, committing to internal controls, board-level oversight, independent external evaluation and shared safety standards. Our members publish safety frameworks, submit models for third-party evaluation and engage with NIST under voluntary agreements today. Codify the outcome Congress wants, one national standard and continued industry-led evaluation, rather than the bureaucracy a small group of advocates has asked for.

We appreciate the bipartisan effort this draft represents, and we would welcome the chance to work with your staffs on a redline before introduction. Please contact Tessa Marchetti, Vice President for Policy, at ACIA.

Respectfully,

Grant Holloway
President and CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance
